## Platform Engineering Scope

> **AI Gateway is the critical path for all AI portfolio delivery.** The AI Gateway is a mandatory pre-condition for any AI use case entering production — no application can route AI inference traffic without it. This means that AI Gateway platform deployment, GOV policy feed activation, SIEM connectivity, and validated operational ownership must all be complete before the first AI use case can go live. Any delay in the AI Gateway delivery track is a delay to the entire AI portfolio. The Enterprise Architecture and AI program leadership SHALL treat the AI Gateway delivery timeline as the binding critical-path constraint on the AI use case roadmap, and SHALL resource it accordingly. Teams SHOULD NOT begin AI application development on the assumption that the AI Gateway will be available by their intended go-live date without a confirmed AI Gateway delivery commitment from the owning platform team.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#ai-gateway-domain-boundary]

### AI Gateway Domain Boundary

The AI Gateway is the AI-specific security enforcement plane. It sits downstream of the enterprise API gateway (which owns TLS, authentication, WAF, and standard HTTP-layer rate limiting) and upstream of model serving endpoints and external AI provider APIs. The AI Gateway's scope is the AI data plane — what happens to inference traffic after it has been authenticated and before it reaches a model.

**ABB Boundary**:
- **AI Gateway governs**: Guardrail and content policy evaluation on prompts and responses; DLP inspection at the AI data plane; token- and cost-aware rate limiting; model routing and provider abstraction; BAA-governed external provider routing; AI-specific audit evidence generation.
- **Enterprise API Gateway governs**: TLS termination, mutual TLS, JWT/OAuth 2.0 authentication, WAF protection, standard HTTP request-rate limiting, and DDoS mitigation. Governed by [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](../../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md).
- **MODEL/INFRA governs**: Model serving infrastructure, inference API security, and GPU/compute platform security. Governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02](../GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02.md) and [GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03](../GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md).
- **GOV governs**: Guardrail policy rule authoring, DLP rule set ownership, BAA allowlist maintenance, capability class taxonomy, and data sensitivity tier registry. Governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](../GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD).
- **Boundary interface**: The `Enterprise API Gateway Handoff` interface (pre-authenticated traffic inbound) and the `Model Routing Dispatch` interface (outbound to model tier) are the AI Gateway's primary architectural seams. The `Guardrail and Policy Feed` interface (inbound from GOV) and `AI Gateway Security Telemetry` interface (outbound to OPS) are its operational dependencies.

### Control Responsibility Matrix

| Control Capability | AI Gateway / Platform Engineering | Enterprise API Gateway Team | GOV Function | OPS / SecOps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AI Gateway platform deployment and lifecycle | **Owns** | — | Reviews policy config | Monitors availability |
| Guardrail policy enforcement runtime | **Owns** (enforcement) | — | **Owns** (rule authoring) | Consumes events |
| DLP inspection runtime | **Owns** (enforcement) | — | **Owns** (rule set ownership) | Consumes events |
| Token and cost rate limiting | **Owns** | Owns HTTP rate limiting (separate) | Sets cost tier thresholds | Consumes cost telemetry |
| Model routing policy configuration | **Owns** (routing runtime) | — | **Owns** (routing rules, BAA allowlist) | Consumes routing events |
| BAA routing enforcement | **Owns** (runtime enforcement) | — | **Owns** (BAA registry, allowlist) | Audits PHI routing events |
| AI audit log generation | **Owns** | — | Consumes for compliance reporting | **Owns** (SIEM ingestion, retention) |
| Policy feed availability | **Owns** (local cache, staleness alerts) | — | **Owns** (feed publication) | Monitors feed health |
| Capability class registry | — | — | **Owns** | — |
| Data sensitivity tier registry | — | — | **Owns** | — |
| Streaming posture configuration | **Owns** | — | Reviews documented posture | — |
| Operational ownership and on-call | **Owns** (designated team TBD at SBB) | — | — | Co-owns incident response |

> **Operational ownership**: The accountable platform team responsible for AI Gateway operations SHALL be designated and documented **before this architecture document is approved for use in production planning** — not deferred to the SBB. The AI Gateway is a fail-closed mandatory enforcement point that carries a SLA obligation covering every AI capability in the enterprise. No team can reasonably accept on-call responsibilities, audit retention obligations, and availability SLA commitments for a system they did not agree to own before it was built. Candidate teams: API Platform Engineering, Security Engineering, AI/ML Platform. **The absence of a designated owning team at the time of document approval is a blocking issue that SHALL be tracked as an open action item against the architecture review record.** The owning team SHALL be named in the SBB and confirmed by the Enterprise Architecture Review Board before production deployment.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#technical-controls-requiring-implementation]

### Technical Controls Requiring Implementation

The following controls are derived from the normative SHALL/SHOULD requirements in [GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07](../GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md). SHOULD-flagged items require documented justification when not implemented.

**Enforcement Pipeline Latency Budget** (applies to all principles):

The 7-stage enforcement pipeline adds in-band overhead to every inference request. Platform Engineering SHALL establish and document an enforcement pipeline latency budget at SBB design time. Recommended targets:

| Application Type | Max Enforcement Pipeline Overhead (p95) | Guardrail Evaluator Selection Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive (chat, real-time summarization, practitioner tools) | 200ms end-to-end across all 7 stages | Fine-tuned safety classifier (10–50ms per evaluation) SHOULD be used; LLM-based meta-evaluator (200–500ms) is unsuitable for this tier |
| Non-interactive / batch | Per documented latency SLA; full buffering acceptable | LLM-based evaluator permissible where latency SLA allows |

The `enforcement_pipeline_latency_ms` audit field SHALL be monitored continuously. A p95 breach of the configured budget SHALL trigger an operational alert. SBB tooling selection SHALL include a measured latency profile under representative production load, not only a capability assessment.

**Principle 1 — AI Gateway as Distinct Enforcement Plane**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL be deployed as a distinct logical component in all service topologies where AI inference traffic is present; co-location with the enterprise API gateway is prohibited.
- The AI Gateway SHALL be the single mandatory enforcement point for all AI inference traffic; direct application-to-model routing SHALL be prohibited at the network layer.
- The AI Gateway SHALL fail closed: unavailability causes requests to be rejected, not routed around enforcement.
- The AI Gateway SHOULD reside in a dedicated network segment, separated from enterprise API gateway and model serving infrastructure.
- The AI Gateway SHOULD be realized using a platform capability that supports policy-as-code deployment.

**Principle 2 — Guardrail and Content Policy Enforcement**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL apply guardrail evaluation to all inbound prompts before forwarding and to all outbound model responses before delivery.
- The AI Gateway SHALL maintain a versioned, centrally managed guardrail policy configuration; policy updates SHALL be applied without requiring application changes.
- The AI Gateway SHALL define and enforce a documented streaming posture: either full-stream buffering before evaluation, or incremental evaluation with documented accuracy limitations and mid-stream termination capability.
- The AI Gateway SHALL return a structured, non-descriptive rejection response on policy block; the specific triggered rule SHALL NOT be disclosed.
- The AI Gateway SHALL record guardrail outcomes per category in the audit log for every evaluated request.

**Principle 3 — Token-Aware and Cost-Aware Rate Limiting**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce token-consumption and cost-based rate limits per authenticated identity, with configurable thresholds per application criticality tier.
- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce concurrent request limits per identity independently of token consumption.
- Rate-limit state SHALL be maintained independently from the enterprise API gateway's HTTP rate-limit state.
- The AI Gateway SHOULD implement request queuing rather than hard rejection for business-critical inference paths on token-limit events.

**Principle 4 — Model Routing and Provider Abstraction**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL route requests based on a centralized routing policy configuration; consuming applications SHALL NOT specify endpoint addresses.
- Data sensitivity tier assignments SHALL be provisioned by GOV; applications SHALL NOT self-assert tier values; unrecognized context identifiers SHALL be treated as the highest sensitivity tier.
- PHI or Regulated PII traffic SHALL be routed only to BAA-covered endpoints; non-BAA routing for PHI SHALL be blocked and logged.
- The AI Gateway SHOULD implement circuit-breaker behavior for sustained endpoint error or latency conditions.
- The AI Gateway SHOULD support a documented experiment routing path (e.g., a designated experiment capability class tier) to enable model canary and A/B testing without requiring a full GOV policy change cycle for each experiment.

**Principle 5 — DLP and PHI Control**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL apply DLP inspection to all inbound prompts (before guardrail evaluation) and all outbound responses.
- The AI Gateway DLP policy SHALL be sourced from the centralized GOV-managed DLP rule set.
- The AI Gateway SHALL NOT forward prompts on the assumption that automated redaction has eliminated all PHI; redaction-as-routing-enabler patterns require CAIO and Privacy Officer risk acceptance documented in the SBB.
- Full prompt or response content containing PHI SHALL NOT appear in standard operational logs; PHI-bearing content SHALL be routed to HIPAA-compliant audit storage only.

**Principle 6 — AI-Specific Audit Evidence Generation**:
- The AI Gateway SHALL generate a structured audit record for every processed inference request, including model version identifier, token counts, routing decision, BAA verification outcome, guardrail outcomes (per category), and DLP outcomes (per category).
- Audit records SHALL be forwarded to the enterprise SIEM in real time or near-real time; forwarding failures SHALL trigger alerts.
- Audit records SHALL be retained for a minimum of six years per HIPAA 45 CFR 164.530(j).
- Audit records SHALL be protected using append-only storage or cryptographic signing.

## Capability Class Taxonomy

The AI Gateway routes requests based on *capability class* — a stable, abstract identifier that consuming applications use to express what kind of AI capability they need, independent of underlying model or provider. Capability class definitions are owned and maintained by the GOV function and published via the policy feed.

The following capability classes represent a reference taxonomy. The GOV function SHALL maintain the authoritative registry; this table is illustrative only.

| Capability Class | Description | Permitted Data Sensitivity | BAA Required |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text-generation-standard` | General-purpose LLM text generation for non-sensitive content | Non-sensitive | No |
| `text-generation-phi` | LLM text generation for workflows involving PHI or Regulated PII | PHI, PII, Non-sensitive | Yes |
| `summarization-standard` | Document or content summarization for non-sensitive content | Non-sensitive | No |
| `summarization-phi` | Document summarization for clinical or member records | PHI, PII, Non-sensitive | Yes |
| `code-generation` | Code generation and completion | Non-sensitive | No |
| `embedding` | Text embedding for semantic search and RAG pipelines | Non-sensitive (PHI variant requires separate class) | No |
| `classification` | Content or entity classification tasks | Non-sensitive | No |
| `experiment` | Designated experiment routing tier — canary, A/B, shadow evaluation for non-sensitive models | Non-sensitive only | No |
| `experiment-phi` | Designated experiment routing tier for model evaluation against real PHI-bearing data; requires elevated approval and time-bounded TTL | PHI, PII, Non-sensitive | Yes |

> **Experiment capability class**: The `experiment` capability class SHOULD be used for model canary deployments and A/B testing against non-sensitive data. It is restricted to non-sensitive data, does not permit PHI routing, and uses a lighter-weight policy update path within the AI Gateway routing configuration. Production traffic SHALL NOT default to the `experiment` class; explicit application opt-in is required. GOV approval is required to create or modify experiment routing entries.

> **`experiment-phi` capability class**: The `experiment-phi` class permits real PHI-bearing data to be used in model evaluation experiments — a necessary capability for healthcare AI use cases where model safety and performance cannot be adequately characterized using synthetic data alone. `experiment-phi` entries SHALL require: (1) joint approval from the CAIO and Privacy Officer; (2) a documented experiment scope, hypothesis, and data handling plan; (3) a mandatory time-bounded TTL not to exceed 90 days without renewal approval; (4) a mandatory post-experiment audit review of all inference traffic processed under the class; and (5) a regulatory review checklist confirming that the experiment does not constitute human subjects research under HIPAA, does not trigger obligations under applicable state AI transparency laws (including Colorado HB 1468 and Illinois AIAA where applicable), and is consistent with CMS guidance on AI in clinical decision support. PHI-bearing experiment traffic SHALL be routed only to BAA-covered endpoints. Production traffic SHALL NOT default to `experiment-phi`; explicit application opt-in with documented approval is required.

> **`experiment-phi` TTL enforcement**: TTL enforcement SHALL be automated — manual GOV expiration is insufficient for a PHI-bearing capability class. The policy feed infrastructure SHALL implement automatic expiration of `experiment-phi` routing entries at TTL: the entry SHALL be removed from the live policy bundle and the AI Gateway SHALL reject requests for the expired entry without requiring a manual GOV action. GOV SHALL configure automated alerts to CAIO and Privacy Officer when an `experiment-phi` entry is within 14 days of TTL expiration, enabling deliberate renewal decisions rather than silent lapses. The post-experiment audit review SHALL be triggered automatically by the TTL expiration event; GOV SHALL track post-experiment audit completion as a required closure step. An `experiment-phi` entry that has reached TTL without a completed audit review SHALL be flagged as an open compliance finding.

## Policy Feed Architecture

The Guardrail and Policy Feed (GOV → AI Gateway) is the operational dependency that keeps the AI Gateway's enforcement posture current. This section defines the expected design of that feed.

> **GOV technology delivery prerequisite**: The policy feed architecture described in this section requires the GOV function to operate purpose-built technology infrastructure — a policy bundle signing infrastructure (PKI or equivalent), a policy feed publication platform (OPA bundle server, Git-backed policy repository, or equivalent), a data sensitivity tier registry store, a capability class registry, and operational workflows for BAA allowlist and DLP rule set management. **This infrastructure does not exist by default** and must be designed, built, and operationally stood up as part of the GOV function's own delivery track. The AI Gateway cannot enforce current policy without it. Before the AI Gateway enters any production planning phase, the implementing team SHALL confirm with the GOV function: (a) which policy feed components are currently operational; (b) which are planned, with committed delivery dates; and (c) the GOV team's capacity model at AI portfolio scale. A GOV function operating at 15+ simultaneous use case onboarding requests with only per-request SLA commitments and no surge capacity plan is a serializing bottleneck risk that must be addressed at the program level, not the architecture level.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#feed-contents]

### Feed Contents

The policy feed published by GOV and consumed by the AI Gateway SHALL include at minimum:

| Feed Component | Description | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrail policy rules | Versioned rule set: harmful content categories, jailbreak patterns, clinical safety guardrails, PHI-topic steering | GOV |

> **Clinical safety guardrail authoring**: Clinical safety guardrail rules cannot be authored by the GOV function alone. Rules that determine whether an AI response is clinically safe or dangerous require clinical subject matter expertise — incorrect rules can block clinically appropriate responses (a patient safety event) or fail to catch clinically dangerous outputs (also a patient safety event). GOV owns the guardrail governance process and policy publication; clinical informatics, medical affairs, or an equivalent clinical SME function SHALL be a required co-author and reviewer for any guardrail rule in the clinical safety category. The CAIO SHALL designate the clinical SME partnership arrangement before the AI Gateway processes any healthcare AI traffic.
| DLP rule set | Versioned DLP patterns: PHI entity types, PII categories, credential patterns, confidential data signatures | GOV |
| BAA provider allowlist | List of external AI providers with active BAA status, provider endpoint identifiers, and effective dates | GOV / Legal |
| Capability class registry | Canonical list of capability classes, permitted data sensitivity tiers, BAA requirement flags | GOV |
| Data sensitivity tier registry | Application context identifier → data sensitivity tier mappings (GOV-provisioned; not application-asserted) | GOV |
| Rate limit tier thresholds | Token and cost cap values per application criticality tier | GOV / AI Gateway Ops |
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#feed-delivery-model]

### Feed Delivery Model

- The policy feed SHOULD be delivered as a versioned, signed artifact (e.g., OPA bundle, JSON policy package with content signature) to enable the AI Gateway to verify feed integrity before applying updates.
- The AI Gateway SHALL maintain a local policy cache to enable continued enforcement during temporary feed unavailability.
- The AI Gateway SHALL track the age of its local policy cache and SHALL generate an operational alert when the cache exceeds the configured maximum staleness window (default: 4 hours; configurable by GOV).
- On feed unavailability, the AI Gateway SHALL continue serving requests against the cached policy unless the cache has exceeded the configured staleness limit, at which point the AI Gateway SHOULD enter a degraded mode with more restrictive default enforcement (e.g., block external provider routing, reduce token limits to a conservative baseline) until feed connectivity is restored.
- On BAA feed unavailability specifically: the AI Gateway SHALL treat the last-known BAA allowlist as authoritative for requests already in-flight; new external provider routing decisions for PHI-classified traffic SHALL be held or blocked until the BAA allowlist can be verified from the feed.
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#illustrative-feed-implementation-options]

### Illustrative Feed Implementation Options

| Approach | Description | Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| OPA (Open Policy Agent) bundle server | GOV publishes policy as OPA bundles; AI Gateway loads bundles on a configured refresh interval; bundles are signed for integrity | Well-supported in Kong, Envoy, and custom gateway implementations; policy-as-code native; bundle signing requires PKI |
| Git-backed policy repository with pull-based sync | Policy rules stored in a version-controlled repository; AI Gateway polls for updates on a configurable interval | Simple to operate; version history and audit trail built in; does not provide push-based immediate updates |
| Managed policy service (AWS, Azure) | AWS Config Rules / Azure Policy for cloud-native gateways; platform-managed distribution | Limited to platform-native gateway integrations; less portable |

### Pattern 1: Guardrail Policy Enforcement — Implementation Guidance

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: All inbound prompts and outbound responses are evaluated against a centralized, versioned guardrail policy before crossing AI data plane boundaries.

**Design considerations**:
- Guardrail evaluation adds in-band latency on every inference request. The guardrail evaluation component should be chosen and configured with this constraint in mind. LLM-based meta-evaluation (using a safety model to judge the prompt) is significantly slower than pattern-based or fine-tuned classifier approaches. For high-throughput or latency-sensitive paths, fine-tuned safety classifiers operating in the 10–50ms range are generally more appropriate than LLM-based evaluators operating in the 200–500ms range.
- The guardrail rule set is owned by GOV and delivered via the policy feed. The AI Gateway platform must support runtime policy updates without requiring a service restart or code deployment.
- Response-path evaluation should be asynchronous where the AI Gateway streaming posture is configured for incremental delivery; the AI Gateway must be capable of injecting a termination signal mid-stream and replacing buffered content with a safe fallback.

**Illustrative tooling**:

| Tooling | Description | Relevant Capability |
|---|---|---|
| Azure AI Content Safety | Managed content safety API — evaluates prompts and responses for harmful content, jailbreak attempts, and protected material | Guardrail evaluation (managed service); supports streaming with partial content evaluation |
| AWS Bedrock Guardrails | Managed guardrails natively integrated with Amazon Bedrock model APIs; supports content filtering, denied topics, and grounding checks | Guardrail evaluation for Bedrock-hosted models; policy configured via Bedrock console or API |
| NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails | Open-source LLM guardrail framework; define guardrail policies in a DSL (Colang); runs as a sidecar or embedded service | Highly configurable; policy-as-code native; requires self-managed deployment |
| Llama Guard / Meta safety models | Open-weight safety classifier fine-tuned for prompt and response classification | Low-latency classifier option; self-hosted; requires MLOps pipeline integration |
| Kong AI Gateway (guardrail plugin) | AI Gateway platform with native support for content safety policy plugins | Integrated guardrail and rate limiting in a single gateway platform |

> **Semantic caching and guardrail enforcement**: Some AI Gateway and API management platforms support semantic caching — returning a stored model response to a semantically similar prompt without re-invoking the model. Semantic caching introduces a risk of guardrail policy bypass: a response evaluated and cached under policy version N may be served after policy version N+1 takes effect, silently bypassing updated guardrail rules. Deployments using semantic caching SHALL adopt the following posture: (a) cached responses SHALL traverse the outbound guardrail and DLP evaluation pipeline on every cache hit — caching eliminates model inference cost, not enforcement cost; (b) the semantic cache SHALL be invalidated on policy bundle version updates; (c) PHI-bearing requests SHALL be excluded from semantic caching entirely; the risk of stale PHI being served to a different user or context is unacceptable. Any deviation from this posture requires explicit documented approval from the CAIO and Privacy Officer.

### Pattern 2: Token Budget and Cost Control — Implementation Guidance

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: Multi-dimensional rate limiting (token count, cost, concurrent requests) is enforced per authenticated identity, independently of enterprise API gateway HTTP rate limiting.

**Design considerations**:
- Token budgeting requires tracking state across requests, which introduces a shared state store dependency. The state store must be highly available — its unavailability should degrade rate limiting to a conservative baseline rather than disable enforcement entirely.
- Input token counting can be estimated pre-dispatch (using a tokenizer matching the target model's tokenization) or retrieved from the model response metadata post-dispatch. Pre-dispatch estimation is necessary for pre-flight limit checks; post-dispatch actuals are required for accurate counter updates.
- Cost estimation requires a configurable cost model (price per input token, price per output token) per capability class and provider. These cost models should be version-controlled alongside capability class definitions in the GOV policy feed.
- For the `experiment` capability class, token and cost counters SHOULD be tracked separately from production counters to enable experiment cost attribution.

**Illustrative tooling**:

| Tooling | Description | Relevant Capability |
|---|---|---|
| Kong AI Gateway (AI Rate Limiting plugin) | Token-aware rate limiting built into Kong's AI Gateway plugin suite; tracks token consumption per consumer | Token and request rate limiting with shared Redis state |
| Azure APIM (AI Token limit policy) | Native token rate limit policy in Azure API Management AI Gateway capabilities | Token rate limiting for Azure OpenAI-backed deployments |
| LiteLLM Proxy | Open-source LLM proxy with built-in token budgeting per user, team, and model; cost tracking via configurable cost model | Token budget, cost tracking, and request routing with PostgreSQL/Redis backend |
| Custom middleware + Redis | Application-level token counter using a Redis sorted set per identity; pre-dispatch tokenizer integration | Fully custom; portable across any AI Gateway platform |

### Pattern 3: BAA-Governed External Provider Routing — Implementation Guidance

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: All outbound requests to external AI providers pass through a centralized, policy-controlled routing layer that enforces BAA routing rules and private connectivity requirements.

**Design considerations**:
- The BAA allowlist must be operationally maintainable. When a provider's BAA expires or is terminated, the AI Gateway must be able to update the allowlist via the policy feed without a service deployment. This requirement effectively mandates dynamic routing policy updates rather than static configuration.
- Private endpoint connectivity (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Endpoints) for BAA-covered external providers eliminates the public internet as a data path for PHI-bearing inference traffic. This is a network architecture constraint that must be addressed during cloud platform design — it cannot be retrofitted into a deployed topology without network changes.
- The AI Gateway should log the private endpoint indicator (whether the request was routed via a private path) as part of every audit record for BAA-governed traffic, to support HIPAA compliance evidence.

**Illustrative tooling**:

| Provider | Private Connectivity Option | BAA Availability |
|---|---|---|
| Azure OpenAI Service | Azure Private Endpoint (via VNet integration) | Available — Microsoft BAA via Azure Online Services Agreement |
| AWS Bedrock | AWS PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint for Bedrock) | Available — AWS BAA via AWS Business Associate Addendum |
| OpenAI API (direct) | No native private endpoint; requires VPN or proxy | BAA available under enterprise agreements; public internet path is default |
| Google Vertex AI | VPC Service Controls + Private Google Access | Available — Google BAA via Google Cloud HIPAA Business Associate Agreement |

> **Note**: Provider BAA availability and private connectivity options change. The GOV function SHALL maintain the authoritative BAA registry and verify BAA status on a minimum annual basis. The table above is illustrative only and SHALL NOT be used as a substitute for the GOV-maintained BAA allowlist.

**Transport security requirements**:

- All outbound connections from the AI Gateway to external AI provider endpoints SHALL enforce a minimum of TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 SHALL be used where the provider supports it, per [GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04 §Principle 6](../GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md). Certificate validation SHALL be enforced; connections to providers presenting self-signed, expired, or revoked certificates SHALL be rejected.
- Providers that do not support private endpoint connectivity (e.g., OpenAI API direct) route over the public internet by default. PHI-classified traffic SHALL NOT be sent to any such provider absent an explicit CAIO and Privacy Officer risk acceptance documented in the SBB. VPN or proxy-based routing for these providers does not substitute for the private endpoint requirement in the ABB; it is a compensating control requiring documented approval.

**AI Gateway outbound credential management**:

- The AI Gateway's own outbound service credentials — API keys and tokens for external AI providers, credentials for the GOV policy feed store, and credentials for the SIEM / audit log destination — SHALL be managed per [GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03 §Principle 6](../GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md) and ADR-SEC-002. Credentials SHALL NOT be stored in container images, configuration files, or pipeline definitions.
- **Cloud-native managed identities** (AWS IAM role for the AI Gateway's compute identity; Azure Managed Identity assigned to the AI Gateway deployment) SHALL be the preferred credential mechanism for any provider that supports them — Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock both support managed identity access. Static API keys are permitted only for providers that do not support managed identity; where used, they SHALL be stored in the enterprise-approved secrets manager with automated rotation enabled and SHALL be injected at runtime.

### Pattern 4: AI Interaction Audit Trail — Implementation Guidance

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: Every inference request produces a structured audit record including token counts, model version, routing decision, BAA verification outcome, guardrail and DLP outcomes, and cost estimate; records are forwarded to SIEM in real time and retained for six years.

**Audit record schema**:

```json
{
  "event_id": "<UUID>",
  "timestamp_ingress": "<ISO8601>",
  "timestamp_egress": "<ISO8601>",
  "requesting_identity": "<user or service identity>",
  "application_context_id": "<GOV-registered identifier>",
  "session_id": "<conversation or session identifier>",
  "data_sensitivity_tier": "phi | pii | non-sensitive",
  "capability_class": "<capability class identifier>",
  "model_endpoint": "<endpoint identifier or provider name>",
  "model_version": "<model version identifier>",
  "baa_routing_rule_applied": "<rule identifier>",
  "baa_verification_outcome": "pass | block | not-applicable",
  "private_endpoint_used": true,
  "input_token_count": 0,
  "output_token_count": 0,
  "estimated_cost_usd": 0.0,
  "request_latency_ms": 0,
  "enforcement_pipeline_latency_ms": 0,
  "dlp_inspection_inbound": {
    "outcome": "pass | block | redact",
    "categories_matched": []
  },
  "guardrail_evaluation_inbound": {
    "outcome": "pass | block",
    "categories_evaluated": [],
    "categories_matched": []
  },
  "rate_limit_check": {
    "outcome": "pass | throttle | block",
    "dimension_triggered": "token | cost | concurrent | none"
  },
  "dlp_inspection_outbound": {
    "outcome": "pass | block | redact",
    "categories_matched": []
  },
  "guardrail_evaluation_outbound": {
    "outcome": "pass | block",
    "categories_matched": []
  },
  "content_context_hash": "<SHA-256 of full assembled prompt as submitted to model — including system message, retrieved context, conversation history, and user message — for cross-system correlation; applications and the AI Gateway MUST hash the same canonical assembled prompt string; partial hashing of only the user message is not sufficient for correlation>",
  "streaming_response": false,
  "streaming_posture_applied": "buffered | incremental | not-applicable",
  "ai_quality_signals": {
    "_note": "AI governance telemetry — routes to GOV-consumed quality data layer, NOT to SIEM security pipeline; all fields nullable",
    "confidence_score": null,
    "groundedness_score": null,
    "rag_grounding_applied": null,
    "user_feedback_rating": null,
    "guardrail_false_positive_flag": null,
    "guardrail_false_positive_appeal_id": null
  }
}
```

**Design considerations**:

- The `enforcement_pipeline_latency_ms` field enables ongoing performance monitoring of the AI Gateway enforcement overhead. OPS SHOULD alert when this field exceeds a defined threshold (recommended baseline: 200ms; adjust per deployment SLA).
- Full prompt and response content SHALL NOT be included in this record. The `content_context_hash` field (SHA-256 of the full assembled prompt as submitted to the model) enables correlation with a HIPAA-compliant audit store without including PHI in the SIEM-bound record. The hash input MUST be the complete assembled prompt — system message, retrieved context, conversation history, and user message — in the exact form submitted to the model. Applications and the AI Gateway must agree on the canonical assembled prompt string; partial hashing (user message only) will break cross-system correlation.
- The `ai_quality_signals` block routes to a GOV-consumed AI governance telemetry stream, distinct from the SIEM-bound security record pipeline. These fields are all nullable; population depends on whether the model provides confidence scores, whether RAG grounding is applied, and whether the application layer provides user feedback signals. The CAIO office is the consumer of this block for responsible AI monitoring purposes.
- For PHI-bearing requests, a parallel record containing full content MAY be written to a separate HIPAA-compliant audit store with appropriate access controls and content-level encryption. This is distinct from the SIEM-bound record and is under OPS custody.
- The `model_version` field is critical for incident investigation and AI governance compliance — it enables reconstruction of exactly which model version produced a given output, which is necessary when models are updated or when a model version is found to have a safety issue post-deployment.

**Illustrative storage and forwarding options**:

| Capability | AWS | Azure |
|---|---|---|
| Append-only audit log (SIEM-bound) | Amazon S3 with Object Lock + Kinesis Firehose to SIEM | Azure Blob Storage with immutability policy + Azure Event Hubs to SIEM |
| HIPAA-compliant full-content audit store | S3 with Object Lock, KMS encryption (HIPAA-eligible key), restricted IAM | Azure Blob with immutability, CMK encryption, Entra RBAC restricted to compliance role |
| Real-time SIEM forwarding | Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose or Kinesis Data Streams | Azure Event Hubs with SIEM connector (Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk) |
| Six-year retention enforcement | S3 Lifecycle policy + Glacier Deep Archive | Azure Blob lifecycle management with archive tier |

### Pattern 5: Cloud Platform Topology — Implementation Guidance

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: The AI Gateway is logically positioned in a dedicated network segment with no direct internet routing, private endpoint connectivity to BAA-governed external AI providers, and network-layer enforcement preventing direct application-to-model routing.

- **Security Groups**: The AI Gateway security group SHALL permit inbound traffic only from the Enterprise API Gateway security group (source-based rule). - **Azure OpenAI Private Endpoints**: Azure OpenAI Service supports Private Endpoints in all commercially available regions. ### Pattern 6: Streaming Response Posture

**Required outcome (from ABB)**: The AI Gateway SHALL define and enforce a documented streaming posture — either full-stream buffering before evaluation, or incremental evaluation with documented accuracy limitations and mid-stream termination capability. Pass-through without evaluation is prohibited.

**Design considerations**:

| Streaming Posture | Description | Latency Impact | Accuracy | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Full buffering** | AI Gateway buffers the complete response stream before applying DLP and guardrail evaluation; delivers the full evaluated response to the consumer | Adds full response generation latency before delivery begins; unsuitable for interactive/chat applications where time-to-first-token matters | Same as non-streaming; full content evaluated | Batch processing, background workflows, non-interactive use cases |
| **Incremental evaluation** | AI Gateway evaluates each chunk or sliding window of the response as it arrives; can terminate and replace the stream on a policy violation | Minimal added latency (evaluation runs concurrently with streaming delivery); time-to-first-token preserved | Reduced: cross-chunk PHI or violations that span window boundaries may be detected late or missed | Interactive applications, chat interfaces, real-time summarization |
| **Chunk accumulation with threshold** | AI Gateway accumulates N tokens before evaluating; delivers evaluated chunks in batches | Partial latency trade-off between full buffering and incremental | Configurable; larger windows improve accuracy | Configurable compromise; recommended for applications with moderate interactivity requirements |

**Recommended defaults by interaction pattern**:

- **Interactive applications** (chat interfaces, care coordinator AI assistants, member-facing chatbots, prior auth workflows): Incremental evaluation with a minimum evaluation window of 64–128 tokens SHOULD be the default streaming posture. Full buffering adds the entire model generation time to the time-to-first-token and is not a deployable user experience for these use cases. Implementations SHALL document the minimum window size, accuracy limitations, and mid-stream termination behavior.
- **Non-interactive / batch / background workflows** (batch summarization, background pipeline processing, compliance-sensitive document workflows): Full buffering SHOULD be the default streaming posture; time-to-first-token is not user-facing and the accuracy advantage of full evaluation justifies the latency.
- **Chunk accumulation with threshold**: Recommended for use cases with moderate interactivity requirements where a 256–512 token window provides acceptable accuracy and latency trade-off.

> **Enterprise AI portfolio note**: The Gainwell AI use case portfolio is weighted toward interactive applications (member-facing, care coordinator, and practitioner tools). Incremental evaluation with a documented minimum window is the expected production configuration for the majority of deployments. Full buffering SHOULD be reserved for explicitly non-interactive use cases.

Incremental evaluation postures SHALL document their minimum evaluation window size and the residual risk of cross-window violation detection failure. Pass-through without evaluation is prohibited in all cases.

**Illustrative tooling support**:

- **Azure AI Content Safety**: Supports streaming content evaluation via the streaming analysis API; provides chunk-by-chunk safety classification with mid-stream termination capability.
- **AWS Bedrock Guardrails**: Supports streaming with `applyGuardrail` API; evaluation applied per-chunk with configurable blocking behavior.
- **Kong AI Gateway**: Streaming support varies by plugin; AI Prompt Guard plugin supports full buffering mode; custom Lua/Python plugins can implement incremental evaluation.
- **LiteLLM Proxy**: Supports full buffering before delivery by setting `stream=False` at the proxy layer regardless of client request; incremental evaluation requires custom callback hooks.

### Deployment Lifecycle

| Phase | Key Activities | Required Inputs from GOV |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-Design: Use Case Approval** | AI use case approval from GOV is required before capability class provisioning or architecture design begins; approval documents the use case purpose, data sensitivity classification, regulatory scope, and responsible AI risk tier per [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](../GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD); no AI Gateway onboarding SHALL proceed without a documented approved use case | Approved use case record; data sensitivity tier assignment |
| Design | Platform selection; network topology design; policy feed integration design; streaming posture decision; operational ownership designation | Capability class registry; data sensitivity tier registry; initial guardrail policy version |
| Platform Deployment | AI Gateway component deployed in dedicated subnet; Security Group / NSG configured; fail-closed behavior verified; private endpoints established | BAA allowlist; DLP rule set; rate limit tier thresholds |
| Policy Integration | Policy feed connectivity established; local cache configured; staleness alert thresholds configured; first policy bundle loaded and verified | Versioned policy bundle; feed signing key |
| Validation | Enforcement pipeline tested end-to-end: rate limiting, DLP block, guardrail block, BAA routing block, fail-closed; audit record schema validated against schema above; SIEM forwarding verified | Test policy rules for validation scenarios |
| Production Readiness | Streaming posture documented; operational runbook complete; on-call ownership designated; SIEM alerting rules active; six-year retention policy applied to audit store | Compliance sign-off from Privacy Officer and CAIO |
| Ongoing Operations | Policy feed health monitored; guardrail effectiveness reviewed quarterly; capability class registry reviewed when new AI use cases onboard; model version tracking in audit records reviewed | Periodic policy bundle updates; BAA renewal notifications |
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#policy-change-management]

### Policy Change Management

Policy changes (guardrail rules, DLP rule sets, BAA allowlist, capability class definitions) flow through GOV and are delivered to the AI Gateway via the policy feed. The following process applies:

1. **Change request**: Policy change requested to GOV (by Security, Privacy, Legal, or AI Platform teams as appropriate to the change type).
2. **Impact assessment**: GOV assesses impact on routing decisions, enforcement outcomes, and any applications using affected capability classes.
3. **Policy bundle update**: GOV publishes a new signed policy bundle version to the feed.
4. **AI Gateway pull and apply**: AI Gateway detects the new bundle version on next poll interval, verifies signature, and applies the update without service restart.
5. **Audit trail**: The policy bundle version applied to each enforcement decision is recorded in the audit record (via the guardrail and DLP outcome fields which reference the evaluated rule set version).

**Experiment routing exception**: For experiment capability class routing entries (model canary / A/B), a lighter-weight change path is available — GOV can update experiment routing entries without a full policy bundle change cycle. Experiment entries are scoped to the `experiment` or `experiment-phi` capability class, and expire automatically after a configurable TTL (`experiment`: default 30 days; `experiment-phi`: default 30 days, maximum 90 days without renewal approval).
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#policy-management-service-levels]

### Policy Management Service Levels

The GOV function is the operational dependency for every AI Gateway policy update. Without defined service levels, GOV becomes a serializing bottleneck as the AI portfolio grows. The following service level guidance applies:

| Operation Type | SHOULD Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Data sensitivity tier assignment (new application context ID) | ≤ 5 business days from request | Required before any application can onboard to AI Gateway |
| Capability class addition (new class) | ≤ 10 business days from request | Requires CAIO review for PHI-tier classes |
| Guardrail rule update (non-clinical) | ≤ 3 business days from approval | Standard policy bundle update cycle |
| Clinical safety guardrail rule update | ≤ 10 business days from approval | Requires clinical SME co-review; see Pattern 1 |
| BAA allowlist update (new provider) | ≤ 5 business days from Legal confirmation of executed BAA | Legal team dependency |
| DLP rule set update | ≤ 5 business days from approval | Standard policy bundle update cycle |
| `experiment` class routing entry | ≤ 2 business days from GOV approval | Lightweight change path |
| `experiment-phi` class routing entry | ≤ 5 business days from CAIO + Privacy Officer approval | Elevated approval required |

The GOV function SHOULD publish actual service level performance metrics quarterly. When a policy cycle is blocking a time-sensitive AI use case, the requesting team MAY escalate to the CAIO for expedited review; the CAIO SHALL have authority to approve a temporary GOV exception with a defined remediation window.

## Compliance Mapping

This section maps ABB normative requirements to implementation patterns in this RAD. For the full compliance framework, see [GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07 §Governance and Compliance](../GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md).

| ABB Requirement | RAD Pattern | Implementation Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrail evaluation — all inbound prompts and outbound responses | Pattern 1 | In-band enforcement; illustrative tooling: Azure AI Content Safety, AWS Bedrock Guardrails, NeMo Guardrails |
| Streaming posture documented and enforced | Pattern 6 | Full buffering default; incremental evaluation supported with documented limitations |
| Token-aware and cost-aware rate limiting | Pattern 2 | State store required; illustrative tooling: LiteLLM, Kong AI Rate Limiting, Azure APIM token limit policy |
| BAA-governed routing via private endpoint | Pattern 3 | PrivateLink (AWS) / Private Endpoints (Azure); BAA allowlist from GOV policy feed |
| Audit record per inference request including model version | Pattern 4 | Full schema defined; SIEM forwarding; HIPAA-compliant parallel store for PHI-bearing content |
| Dedicated network segment, fail-closed | Pattern 5 | AWS / Azure topology guidance; Security Group / NSG source restriction |
| GOV-managed policy feed | Feed Architecture section | OPA bundle or Git-backed; signed for integrity; local cache with staleness alerting |
| Capability class taxonomy (no application self-routing) | Capability Class Taxonomy section | GOV-owned registry; `experiment` and `experiment-phi` classes for canary/A/B |

## Known Limitations and SBB Design Requirements

The following limitations apply to this RAD and must be addressed during SBB design before the AI Gateway enters production deployment in affected environments.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#multi-tenancy-and-program-level-isolation]

### Multi-Tenancy and Program-Level Isolation

This RAD treats the AI Gateway as a single-tenant enterprise service. The following components are specified as enterprise-wide artifacts without program-level scoping:

- **BAA allowlist** — a single list without program scope; if Program A has a BAA with Provider X and Program B does not, the current design does not enforce program-level BAA scope at routing time
- **Guardrail policy rules** — a single rule set; clinical safety guardrails appropriate for one program may be inapplicable or incorrect for another
- **DLP rule set** — a single rule set without program-scoped policy variations
- **Audit log stream** — a single telemetry stream; audit records from Program A and Program B are not segregated at the AI Gateway tier
- **Token and cost rate limits** — tier thresholds apply enterprise-wide; program-level cost attribution requires additional counter instrumentation

Gainwell operates across multiple state programs and business lines with distinct contractual, regulatory, and data segregation requirements. **A shared AI Gateway deployment serving multiple programs cannot use this RAD as a turnkey deployment guide without additional SBB-level design work addressing program-level policy scoping, audit log segregation, and BAA allowlist scoping per program.** The SBB for any multi-program AI Gateway deployment SHALL include a program isolation design addendum reviewed by Legal, Privacy, and the CAIO office.
page_texts.30:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#service-to-service-and-programmatic-ai-traffic]

### Service-to-Service and Programmatic AI Traffic

This RAD and the paired ABB define the primary inbound authentication model for human-origin application traffic forwarded by the enterprise API gateway. Backend services, batch processors, and event-driven pipelines operating under machine identities (service accounts, managed identities) represent a distinct traffic class that may not pass through the enterprise API gateway and does not carry a user bearer token.

The following requirements apply to machine-origin AI Gateway callers and SHALL be addressed in the SBB:

| Requirement | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Authentication mechanism | Machine-origin callers SHALL authenticate using **RFC 8705 mutual-TLS (certificate-bound access tokens)**. In containerised environments, **SPIFFE/SPIRE SVIDs** are the required workload identity mechanism, per [GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12](../../Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12.md). Short-lived OAuth 2.0 client credentials with RFC 9449 DPoP are a compensating mechanism where mTLS is not achievable; the SBB SHALL document the justification |
| Enforcement pipeline | Machine-origin callers SHALL traverse the same 7-stage enforcement pipeline as human-origin callers; the SBB SHALL confirm that no enforcement stage is bypassed for machine identities |
| Service identity enrollment | Machine-origin caller service identities SHALL be enrolled in the GOV-managed application context registry; unenrolled machine callers SHALL be treated as unrecognised context identifiers and routed at the highest sensitivity tier |
| Token budget assignment | The SBB SHALL define per-identity token and cost rate limits for machine-origin callers; machine-origin callers SHOULD NOT share rate-limit counters with human-origin callers from the same application |
| Audit record identity fields | Audit records for machine-origin traffic SHALL capture the enrolled service identity in the `requesting_identity` field; generic or anonymous service account identifiers are not acceptable |

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#gov-function-operational-readiness]

### GOV Function Operational Readiness

This RAD assigns the following operational capabilities to the GOV function: guardrail rule authoring and publication, DLP rule set management, BAA allowlist maintenance, capability class registry management, data sensitivity tier registry management, rate limit threshold management, policy bundle signing and publication, and clinical safety guardrail co-authorship with clinical SMEs. Before the AI Gateway enters production deployment, the implementing team SHALL confirm with the GOV function which of these capabilities are currently operational and which are planned. Capabilities not yet operational in GOV are dependencies that must be resolved before the AI Gateway can be deployed against the affected enforcement stages. See [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](../GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD) for the authoritative GOV capability scope.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#data-sensitivity-tier-mapping]

### Data Sensitivity Tier Mapping

The three-tier data sensitivity model used in this RAD (`phi`, `pii`, `non-sensitive`) is a routing proxy, not the authoritative enterprise data classification scheme. The authoritative classification scheme is defined in the DATA domain ([GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01](../GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md)) and is more granular — distinguishing de-identified data, limited datasets, fully-identified PHI, Regulated PII, general PII, and confidential business information among others. The GOV function SHALL define and publish the canonical mapping from the enterprise classification scheme to the three routing tiers before data sensitivity tier registry entries are provisioned. Without this mapping, application teams cannot reliably determine the correct tier for their use case.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#ha-topology-and-availability-sla]

### HA Topology and Availability SLA

This RAD does not specify an HA deployment topology or an availability SLA for the AI Gateway. Because the AI Gateway is a fail-closed mandatory enforcement point, its availability determines the availability ceiling of every AI capability it serves. The SBB SHALL define the HA topology (active-active or active-passive), the target availability SLA, the RTO/RPO, and the degraded-mode routing policy for partial enforcement pipeline failures. These decisions SHALL be reviewed by the AI Gateway operational owner and the CAIO before the AI Gateway is placed on any clinical decision support or member-facing critical path.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md#business-continuity-and-disaster-recovery]

### Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery

The AI Gateway is a fail-closed mandatory enforcement point. An extended regional outage affecting the AI Gateway causes all AI capabilities to go dark for the duration. For AI capabilities on a clinical decision support or member-facing critical path, this creates operational and patient safety risk that requires a documented BCM posture.

The SBB SHALL define and document the following for any AI Gateway deployment serving critical-path AI capabilities:

| BCM Element | Required Disposition |
|---|---|
| Regional outage posture | Explicit documented choice: (a) AI capabilities go dark for the duration of the outage (acceptable for non-critical-path use cases only); (b) a DR failover site operates a secondary AI Gateway instance with independent policy feed connectivity; or (c) a declared exception process permits a time-bounded bypass under a named incident commander during a confirmed regional outage event |
| RTO / RPO targets | Defined per clinical criticality tier; clinical decision support AI capabilities with patient safety implications SHOULD have RTO targets consistent with the SLA of the clinical workflow they support |
| DR instance policy sync | Where a secondary AI Gateway instance is deployed for DR, it SHALL receive the same signed policy bundle feed as the primary; policy divergence between primary and DR instances is not acceptable |
| Bypass exception process | If a time-bounded bypass is selected as the DR posture, the exception process SHALL be documented in the operational runbook, SHALL require CAIO and CISO authorization, and SHALL impose a maximum bypass window after which traffic is rejected pending recovery |
| BCM testing | The selected BCM posture SHALL be tested at minimum annually; test results SHALL be reviewed by the CAIO and operational owner |

> PHI-bearing use cases on clinical decision support paths are subject to HIPAA business continuity requirements under §164.308(a)(7) (Contingency Plan). The BCM posture selected for AI capabilities in those paths must be evaluated against those requirements by the Privacy Officer and relevant compliance contacts.
